title: Introduce yourself
subtitle: Unit 1: five sentences you will use everywhere

steps.title: Four short sentences
steps.body:
You can introduce yourself with four short sentences. Learn them as blocks, exactly as you hear them. The grammar behind them comes in the next lesson.

Je m'appelle literally means I call myself. It is how French says my name is.

steps.tip: Say zhuh ma-PELL, then your own name.
A man says canadien. The ending is nasal, and the n is not pronounced. Next you hear the feminine form.
The same sentence, said by a woman. Now the n at the end is pronounced: ka-na-DYEN.
Say zhuh PARL. The last e of parle is silent.
J'habite sounds like zha-BEET. The h is silent.

steps.prompt: How do you say My name is Sam?
steps.explain: Je m'appelle means my name is. The other two sentences mean I live in Sam and I speak Sam.
Parle means speak. Je parle français means I speak French.

steps.question: Where does the speaker live?
steps.explain: À Montréal means in Montréal. The h in j'habite is silent.

steps.question: What does the speaker say about themselves?
steps.explain: Canadienne means Canadian, said by a woman. Je suis means I am.

steps.title: Nice to meet you
steps.body:
When you meet someone, say enchanté. It means nice to meet you.

A man writes enchanté. A woman writes enchantée, with one more e. You say both exactly the same way: ahn-shahn-TAY.

examples.en: Nice to meet you (written by a man).
Nice to meet you (written by a woman).

steps.tip: The same sound for a man or a woman: ahn-shahn-TAY.

steps.prompt: Which sentence says where you live?
steps.explain: J'habite à means I live in. The other sentences say who you are and what you speak.

steps.title: Next: why these sentences work
steps.body: In the next lesson you learn the small grammar behind them: je suis, tu es, and when to say tu or vous.
